Abstract
Objective  Low dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening has been proven to be effective in reducing lung 
cancer mortality, but the ensuing high false-positive and overdiagnosis rates shackle the effectiveness of lung cancer 
screening (LCS) in China. Nodule malignancy prediction models may be an applicable solution.
Methods  We conducted a prospective cohort study to develop and internally validate the model using data from 
the ongoing Henan province Cancer Screening Program in Urban China (CanSPUC). From 2013 to 2021, 23,031 heavy 
smokers underwent baseline screening with LDCT; 2553 participants were diagnosed with pulmonary nodules. 
Detailed questionnaire, physical assessment and follow-up were completed for all participants. Multivariable Cox 
proportional risk regression models were used to identify and integrate key prognostic factors for the development of 
a nomogram model. Data from the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) were utilized for external validation.
Results  A total of 111 lung cancer cases with a median follow-up duration of 3.7 years occurred in the Henan 
CanSPUC. Age, gender, physical activity, consumption of pickled food, history of silicosis or pneumoconiosis, nodule 
type, size, calcification, and pleural retraction sign were included into the model. The AUC was 0.855, 0.844, and 0.863 
for the 1-, 3- and 5-year lung cancer risk in the training set, respectively. Compared with Mayo model, VA model, 
PKU model, and Brock model, the Henan CanSPUC model yield statistically better discriminatory performance (all 
P values < 0.05). The model calibrated well across the deciles of predicted risk in both the overall population and all 
subgroups. The model demonstrated good calibration and discrimination in the internal validation cohort, while the 
external validation cohort showed lower predictive performance, indicating that further external validation is needed.
Conclusions  The model developed and validated in this study may be used to estimate the probability of lung 
cancer in nodules detected at baseline LDCT, allowing more efficient risk-adapted follow-up in population-based LCS 
programs. However, further external validation in broader and more diverse populations is warranted.

Introduction
Lung cancer ranks as the third most often diagnosed dis­
ease worldwide and is the primary cause of cancer-related 
fatalities, resulting in 1.8  million deaths annually [1]. 
Despite ongoing advancements in lung cancer treatment, 
a previous national study has shown a 5-year survival rate 
of 18% for lung cancer patients in China [2]. Early detec­
tion and treatment are one of the indispensable measures 
to reduce the disease burden of lung cancer. Meta-anal­
yses and randomized controlled studies have definitively 
proven that screening high-risk patients who have a his­
tory of smoking using low-dose computed tomography 
(LDCT) significantly reduces death from lung cancer [3, 
4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Lung cancer CT screening initiatives have 
been established at the national or regional scale in some 
regions of Asia, including China [10, 11].
The widespread use of LDCT scans has also resulted 
in the improved detection of lung nodules [12]. While 
the majority of nodules, over 95%, are noncancerous 
[7], the identification of a lung nodule can still cause 
significant concern for both patients and physicians, as 
it raises the possibility of lung cancer and the challenge 
of distinguishing between benign and malignant nod­
ules. Practice guidelines intend to optimize the benefits 
of detecting cancer at an early stage while minimizing 
the harms of potential over-diagnoses by adjusting the 
screening intervals according to the risk profile. Statisti­
cal models have been developed to predict lung cancer 
risk and identify individuals who might be safely assigned 
to biennial screening [13]. One such model is the Lung 
Cancer Risk Assessment Tool (LCRAT) + CT, which 
combines individual risk factors with CT image features 
[14, 15].
Before recently, population-based data on screen-
detected lung nodules among Chinese was unavailable 
[16, 17]. Expert opinion and studies of select popula­
tions with a high prevalence of lung cancer have helped 
fill gaps in knowledge in this field [18, 19, 20]. Guidelines 
have had to make recommendations with inadequate 
data, and prediction models may not work consistently 
across different care settings and populations [21]. In this 
study, we sought to develop a prediction model that uses 
LDCT imaging features of a presumed nonmalignant 
lung nodule to forecast the detection of lung cancer in 
one year, three years, and five years based on a popula­
tion-based cohort study in Henan, China, validate them 
in the multicenter National Lung Screening Trial (NLST).
Methods
Data sources and study population
This was a prospective cohort study that aimed to 
develop and internally validate a lung cancer risk pre­
diction model in a population of high-risk individuals 
undergoing LDCT screening. For model development 
and internal validation dataset, we used data acquired 
from a nationwide population-based cancer screening 
program named the Cancer Screening Program in Urban 
China (CanSPUC) initiated from 2012 and funded by the 
Ministry of Finance and the National Health Commission 
of China. The study targeted residents aged 40 to 74, with 
a specific focus on the five types of most prevalent cancer 
in urban China, including lung cancer, female breast can­
cer, liver cancer, upper gastrointestinal tract cancer, and 
colorectal cancer. The details of the CanSPUC could be 
found in previously published articles [11].
The study incorporates data obtained from the CanS­
PUC Program in Henan province between October 2013 
and December 2021. The research included a total of 8 
cities: Zhengzhou, Zhumadian, Anyang, Luoyang, Nan­
yang, Jiaozuo, Puyang, and Xinxiang. The trained staff 
conducted interviews with all eligible participants to 
gather data on their exposure to risk variables and assess 
their cancer risk using a well-established scoring meth­
odology [22]. We used the standardized interview pro­
tocol published by Li et al. [10]. In the current screening 
program, only individuals deemed to be at a high risk of 
developing lung cancer were advised to undergo a free 
LDCT examination at a specialized hospital designated 
by the program [11].
The research tracked participants from their first atten­
dance at the baseline evaluation until the cancer diagno­
sis, death, loss to follow-up, or administrative censoring 
(June 2022), whichever comes first. During the study 
period, more cases of lung cancer were collected via the 
implementation of follow-up interviews conducted by 
telephone or in-person. In addition, the participants’ 
information was cross-checked with the provincial can­
cer registry database. Institutional review boards at the 
National Cancer Center/Cancer Hospital, Chinese Acad­
emy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical 
College, as well as Henan Cancer Hospital approved the 
study, and each participants provided written consent to 
participate in the study. We followed the Strengthening 
the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology 
(STROBE) reporting criteria.
LDCT examination and nodules definition
All subjects underwent LDCT using a 16-slice multi­
detector CT (LightSpeed-16, GE, America). The pro­
tocol parameters were 120 KVp and 30 mAs for LDCT, 
512 × 512 matrix, field of view 400 mm × 400–500 mm 
× 500 mm, collimation 128 × 0.625 mm or 16 × 1.25 mm, 
rotation 0.5  s, pitch 0.8 or 1.02, 1.25  mm slice width 
with 1.25 mm reconstruction interval, and scan duration 
3–10  s. Unenhanced spiral images were acquired with 
breath-hold from the thoracic inlet to the lung bases. 
Images were reconstructed using a standard algorithm. 
All images were sent to a GE ADW 4.5 workstation and

underwent multiplanar reconstruction (mipPR). All stud­
ies were reviewed on a PACS workstation with a window 
height of -500 to -700 HU and a width of 1400 HU.
Nodule size and density were defined according to the 
Fleischner Society guidelines [23]. Each baseline LDCT 
scan was originally read and reported by two of the 
thoracic radiologists with 9 and 15 years of experience, 
respectively. The number, size and characteristics of the 
nodules were recorded in structured reports. Nodules 
were measured on lung window images using manual 
calipers at the largest nodule area for both long and short 
axis diameters. The average of the two diameters was 
reported. For part-solid nodules, the diameters of the 
whole nodule and the solid component were reported. 
Baseline CT evaluations were defined as positive if solid 
or part-solid nodules ≥ 5 mm in diameter, non-solid nod­
ules ≥ 8 mm, or intratracheal nodules were detected.
Assessment of covariate
To identify potential risk factors for lung cancer, the fol­
lowing data were collected through self-reports, catego­
rized into six main areas:
(1)	Demographic characteristics: This includes age, 
gender, race, level of education, marriage, height, 
and weight. Education level was categorized as 
low (primary school or below), medium (junior or 
senior high school), and high (undergraduate or 
higher). Body Mass Index (BMI) was calculated using 
height and weight and classified into the following 
categories: underweight (< 18.5 kg/m²), normal 
weight (18.5–23.9 kg/m²), overweight (24.0–27.9 kg/
m²), and obese (≥ 28.0 kg/m²).
(2)	Dietary habit: (a) Taste preferences: Data were 
collected on the intake of hot foods, high-salt foods, 
and high-fat diets, categorized as either “no” or “yes”. 
(b) Pickled food consumption: Frequency of pickled 
food consumption over the past two years was 
assessed using a scale from 0 to 3 days per week to 
4–7 days per week.
(3)	Living environment, behavior and habits: (a) 
Cooking oil fume (COF) exposure: Exposure 
was categorized based on the use of cooking 
technologies, where “none or a little” exposure 
indicated the use of chimneys, fume extractors, 
or smokeless pots during cooking, while “a lot” 
signified their absence. (b) Smoking status: Smoking 
behavior was classified as “current” if the individual 
smoked more than once a day for at least six months, 
“former” if they had quit, and “never” if they had 
never smoked. (c) Alcohol consumption: Individuals 
who consumed alcohol at least once a week for 
more than six months were categorized as “current 
drinkers”, those who had quit as “former drinkers”, 
and those who never drank alcohol were categorized 
as “never drinkers”.d) Physical activity: Activities 
were categorized into Taijiquan/Qigong/Walking, 
long-distance running/aerobics, ball games (e.g., 
basketball, table tennis, badminton), fast walking/
yangko dance, swimming, and other forms of 
exercise (e.g., mountain climbing, rope skipping, 
shuttlecock kicking). Those who engaged in physical 
activity for at least three days a week with a total 
duration of ≥ 90 min were classified as engaging in 
“heavy physical activity”; others were categorized as 
having “moderate or no physical activity”.
(4)	Comorbidities: Self-reported comorbid conditions 
included chronic respiratory diseases such as 
tuberculosis, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, 
asthma, bronchiectasis, silicosis, pneumoconiosis, as 
well as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes. 
These conditions required confirmation through a 
diagnosis by a professional medical institution.
(5)	First-degree family history of lung cancer: This 
category examined whether the subject had a first-
degree relative (parent or sibling) diagnosed with 
lung cancer.
(6)	Pulmonary nodules: Information on the 
characteristics of pulmonary nodules was recorded, 
including size, location (left upper lobe, left lower 
lobe, right upper lobe, right middle lobe, and right 
lower lobe), type (solid, part-solid, nonsolid), border 
definition (clear, unclear), presence of calcification 
(yes or no), and pleural retraction sign (yes or no).
Efficacy evaluation of the CanSPUC model
In our assessment of the model’s performance, we first 
randomly divided the 2553 lung nodule patients into 
training and validation datasets, maintaining an approxi­
mate 1:1 ratio. Subsequently, the CanSPUC model’s effi­
cacy was assessed using the internal validation dataset. 
To further benchmark the CanSPUC model, we tested 
four widely recognized lung cancer prediction models 
(the Mayo model [24], the Veterans Affairs (VA) model 
[25], the PKU model [26], and the Brock model [27]) on 
the training set, comparing their performance with that 
of the CanSPUC model.
External validation datasets
For model validation, we used US National Lung Screen­
ing Trial (NLST) data (n = 10,251) [7]. The NLST was a 
randomised controlled trial of lung cancer screening 
comparing CT against chest radiography in 33 US cen­
ters between 2002 and 2004 with follow-up through 2009 
[28]. Participation in the NLST was restricted to those 
considered at high risk of developing lung cancer: a 30 
pack-year smoking history and, if a participant who pre­
viously smoked, having quit within 15 years of enrolment.

LDCT and were found non-calcified nodule/mass ≥ 4 mm 
on any screen.
Statistical analysis
Data were analyzed from March to September 2024. The 
mean ± standard errors were used to portray continu­
ous variables, whereas counts (percentages) were used 
to present categorical variables. Analysis of variance 
(ANOVA) were used to compare basic characteristics for 
continuous and categorical variables.
In this study, Person-years were calculated from the 
date of the baseline to the date of diagnosis, death, loss 
to follow-up, or the end of follow-up, whichever occurred 
first. In addition, to account for potential confounding 
factors, we constructed a nomogram based on all inde­
pendent prognostic factors selected by stepwise mul­
tivariate Cox regression (Pentry = 0.15, Pstay = 0.10) to 
estimate the 1-, 3-, and 5-year lung cancer risk in the 
training set [29]. To assess the discriminatory perfor­
mance, we used receiver operating characteristic (ROC) 
curve analysis. We provided the areas under the curve 
(AUCs) with 1,000 bootstrap bias-corrected 95% confi­
dence intervals (CI). Using DeLong and colleagues’ non­
parametric technique [30], we compared differences in 
AUCs. We showed the actual and expected cancer rates 
by decile of predicted likelihood to evaluate calibration.
Statistical analyses were performed using R (version 
4.0.3; R Foundation for Statistical Computing) and SAS 
(version 9.4; SAS Institute) software. The nomogram was 
generated with the rms package, while the receiver oper­
ating characteristic curves were constructed using the 
survivalROC package. A calibration curve was plotted 
using the ggplot2 package.
Results
Participant characteristic
A total of 23,031 individuals at high risk for lung can­
cer were enrolled for LDCT screening. After excluding 
participants without pulmonary nodules (n = 20,465) 
and those with missing data (n = 13), a total of 2,553 
patients were included in this study. They were randomly 
divided into the training set (n = 1,273) and validation 
set (n = 1,280). The participant selection flowchart is 
shown in Fig. 1. e-Table 1 displays the attributes of the 
people who were included in the training and validation 
cohort. In the training cohort, lung cancer cases were 
more frequently observed among individuals who were 
older, female, consumed pickled foods, had lower levels 
of physical activity, a history of chronic respiratory dis­
eases, tuberculosis, emphysema, or asthma bronchiecta­
sis, as well as those with non-solid nodules, well-defined 
margins, non-calcified nodules, and pleural indentation 
sign. In the internal validation cohort, lung cancer cases 
were more common among individuals with a history of 
asthma bronchiectasis, non-solid nodules, well-defined 
margins, non-calcified nodules, and pleural indentation 
sign. In the external validation cohort, lung cancer cases 
were more frequently associated with older age, lower 
educational levels, lower body mass index, a smoking his­
tory, a history of chronic respiratory diseases, and a first-
degree family history of lung cancer.
Development of the lung Cancer risk assessment model
Table  1 lists the hazard ratios (HRs) with 95%CI for 
each predictor factor in the training set. We found that 
age (50–59 years: HR 3.30, 95% CI 0.77–14.09; 60–69 
years: HR 1.53, 95%CI 0.34–6.84; 70–74 years: HR 5.25, 
95% CI 1.06–25.95), gender (female: HR 1.75, 95% CI 
0.94–3.28), pickled food (4–7 days/week: HR 1.89, 95%CI 
1.03–3.49), Moderate or no physical activity (HR 1.75, 
95% CI 0.85–3.63), history of silicosis or pneumoconiosis 
(HR 3.68, 95% CI 1.58–8.58), nodule type (Part-solid: HR 
3.19, 95%CI 1.53–6.67; Nonsolid: HR 4.52, 95%CI 2.21–
9.24), non-calcified (HR 5.34, 95% CI 0.72–39.66), pleural 
retraction sign (HR 2.15, 95% CI 1.02–4.52), and nodule 
size (HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.05–1.10) were independent risk 
factors for lung cancer. Therefore, we used these variables 
to construct the model and plotted the nomogram for 
predictin g lung cancer risk at 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year 
intervals (Fig. 2).
Predictive performance of the model
Figure 3 depicts the lung cancer incidence rates across 
different cancer risk categories. After dividing partici­
pants into three groups (low risk, moderate risk, and 
high risk) based on the predicted lung cancer risk from 
the model, we found that the event-free score in the low-
risk group was statistically significantly higher than in the 
moderate and high-risk groups.
The ROC curve of the prediction model is shown in 
Fig.  4. In the training set, the AUC for predicting lung 
cancer risk at 1 year, 3 years, and 5 years was 0.855, 0.844, 
and 0.863, respectively. The calibration curve of the 
nomogram, shown in e-Figure 1, indicates that the model 
exhibits good calibration across the deciles of predicted 
risk in the training set.
Comparison of the CanSPUC model with four other models
The predictive performance of the five models is shown 
in e-Figure 2. From the ROC curve analysis of the train­
ing set, we found that the CanSPUC model significantly 
outperformed the Mayo, VA, PKU, and Brock models. 
We further plotted the probability distribution of lung 
cancer across different models (e-Figure 3). The figure 
shows that, compared to the other models, the CanS­
PUC model was able to distinguish between malignant 
and benign nodules within a narrower probability range,

Validation of the lung Cancer risk model
The ROC curve of the prediction model in the valida­
tion set is shown in Fig. 5. In the internal validation set 
(Fig.  5A), the AUC for predicting lung cancer risk at 
1 year, 3 years, and 5 years was 0.726, 0.745, and 0.773, 
respectively. In the external validation set (Fig. 5B), the 
AUC for predicting lung cancer risk at 1 year, 3 years, and 
5 years was 0.732, 0.656, and 0.637, respectively. The cali­
bration curves for the 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year lung can­
cer risk prediction nomograms in the validation sets (A: 
internal validation; B: external validation) are shown in 
e-Figure 4. The results from both the internal and exter­
nal validation sets were similar and supported the predic­
tive performance of the model.
Discussions
In this study, we used data from a large lung cancer 
screening cohort study to develop a lung cancer risk pre­
diction model for patients with lung nodules. The model 
was based on nine variables, including demographics 
(age, gender), lifestyle (physical activity), dietary habits 
(pickled food), previous lung disease (history of silico­
sis or pneumoconiosis), and lung nodule characteristics 
(nodule type, nodule size, calcification, and pleural con­
striction sign). The model has been internally validated 
and externally validated by the NLST, and the results 
show that the model has good discriminatory accuracy 
for patients with pulmonary nodules.
For patients with lung nodules, several risk factors for 
lung cancer have been identified, including demographics 
(age, gender) [31], dietary habits (consumption of pickled 
foods) [32], lifestyle (history of smoking, history of alco­
hol consumption) [33], previous lung disease (history of 
silicosis or pneumoconiosis) [34], and nodule charac­
teristics (type of nodule [25, 27], size [25, 27, 35], calci­
fication [33, 36], and pleural constriction sign) [24, 37]. 
The risk factors for lung cancer identified in this study, 
such as age, sex, and history of silicosis or pneumoco­
niosis, are consistent with the results of previous stud­
ies. Meanwhile, our study showed that advanced age is 
an important risk factor for lung cancer in patients with

lung nodules, with the risk in the 70–74 age group being 
more than five times higher than that in the 40–49 age 
group. In addition, as in other studies, we found that the 
incidence of lung cancer in non-solid nodules was much 
higher than that in solid nodules [27].
To facilitate early detection and effective screening of 
lung cancer, numerous lung cancer risk prediction mod­
els based on lung nodules have been developed in recent 
years. However, due to differences in population charac­
teristics, geographic environment, lifestyle, dietary hab­
its, and research design, different populations often yield 
divergent results. Therefore, to assess the lung cancer 
risk of lung nodule patients more accurately in specific 
regions and provide actionable management recom­
mendations for clinicians and patients, this study com­
bines patient characteristics, lifestyle, dietary habits, and 
imaging examination results to develop a new prediction 
model. Additionally, the performance of four previously 
published models was validated. The model was con­
structed using the training set, and its discriminatory 
ability was compared with that of the other four models 
using the area under the ROC curve (AUC). Typically, 
the closer the AUC is to 1, the stronger the model’s ability 
to distinguish between lung cancer patients and non-lung 
cancer patients. In this study, the CanSPUC model 
achieved a AUC of 0.857 in the training cohort, signifi­
cantly outperforming the Mayo model (AUC = 0.754), 
VA model (AUC = 0.748), PKU model (AUC = 0.778), 
and Brock model (AUC = 0.824) when validated in the 
same training cohort. Furthermore, we compared the 
malignant probability distributions of different models, 
and the CanSPUC model demonstrated superior perfor­
mance in distinguishing between benign and malignant 
nodules. Clearly, the proposed CanSPUC model is more 
suitable for predicting lung cancer risk in lung nodule 
patients in this region. It is important to note that these 
models were developed based on the characteristics of 
specific regional populations, and thus have limitations 
in their applicability. Specifically, the Mayo model is not 
suitable for patients diagnosed with cancer or with a his­
tory of lung cancer [24]; the VA model is not applicable 
to nodules smaller than 7  mm [25]; the PKU model is 
not applicable to patients with a history of pulmonary or 
extra-pulmonary malignancies [26]; and the Brock model 
is neither suitable for screening low-risk populations nor 
for patients with hilar or mediastinal lymph node disease 
[27]. Therefore, when existing prediction models fail to 
provide adequate management recommendations for

patients, the development of regional prediction models 
tailored to specific populations is essential.
In order to assess the predictive power of the Henan 
CanSPUC model more realistically and to determine 
whether the Henan CanSPUC model can be generalized 
to a new population, we actively pursued external valida­
tion. NLST, a large-scale randomized study of lung can­
cer screening in a high-risk population, is an ideal tool 
for external validation [7, 28]. Our results of external 
validation with the NLST dataset found that the AUC of 
subjects’ lung cancer risk in the NLST dataset, although 
reduced compared with the AUC of subjects’ lung cancer 
risk in the training set, still performed well in predicting 
the 1-year lung cancer risk of subjects, which indicates 
that the Henan CanSPUC model has some generaliza­
tion ability but the predictive ability when performing 
long-term lung cancer risk prediction may decrease, 
which may be related to the fact that the accuracy of the 
model is susceptible to factors such as the characteristics 
of the target population and the prevalence of malignant 
tumors [25].
A major strength of this study is that the prediction 
model we developed is based on a large-scale population-
based cancer screening program in mainland China. In 
addition, we comprehensively assessed multiple lung 
cancer-related risk factors and identified multiple inde­
pendent predictors, aiming to improve the accuracy 
of lung cancer risk prediction from multiple perspec­
tives. And the model has been externally validated in 
the large randomized controlled trial NLST, which not 
only serves as a practical tool to triage high-risk patients 
among lung nodule patients, but also further guides pub­
lic health measures and provides a basis for lung nodule 
management. Standardized data collection protocols 
and trained interviewers were used to minimize infor­
mation bias, while the prospective cohort design helped 
mitigate selection bias. However, there are some limi­
tations in this study, such as some of the self-reported 
data may be affected by recall bias, and the information 
about nodule type, size, calcification, and pleural con­
striction signs in our study was collected from radiologic 
reports rather than directly from CT imaging, which may 
reduce the accuracy of model prediction if inaccurate 
and incomplete information is present; Another limi­
tation is the potential for selection bias, as participants 
in this screening program were self-selected or referred 
based on perceived high risk, and may not represent the 
general population. This could limit the generalizability 
of our findings. Additionally, despite being developed 
from a large cohort, the relatively small number of lung 
cancer cases in the training set (n = 49) compared to the 
number of predictive factors may have led to overfitting 
and limited generalizability. This limitation is reflected 
in the lower predictive performance in the internal and

predictions. Additionally, the absence of some predic­
tive variables in the external validation dataset may have 
further reduced the accuracy of the model’s predictions. 
Although the CanSPUC model showed superior perfor­
mance compared to the four other models in the training 
set, this comparison was not extended to the internal and 
external validation sets due to the lack of some predic­
tive variables required by the other models in the vali­
dation data. This limitation should be considered when 
interpreting the comparative performance of the models. 
What’s more, we did not perform subgroup or sensitivity 
analyses in this study, which limits our ability to evaluate 
the robustness of the model’s performance in different 
subpopulations.
Conclusions
In summary, using data from a large-scale lung cancer 
screening program in China, we created and validated a 
predictive model for assessing lung cancer risk in patients 
with pulmonary nodules. The model shows robust dis­
criminatory capacity within the study cohort, but given 
the poorer performance in the external validation, fur­
ther validation studies in broader and more diverse popu­
lations are necessary to confirm its generalizability and 
potential utility in clinical practice.

Abstract: Objective Low dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening has been proven to be effective in reducing lung cancer mortality, but the ensuing high false-positive and overdiagnosis rates shackle the effectiveness of lung cancer screening (LCS) in China. Nodule malignancy prediction models may be an applicable solution. Methods We conducted a prospective cohort study to develop and internally validate the model using data from the ongoing Henan province Cancer Screening Program in Urban China (CanSPUC). From 2013 to 2021, 23,031 heavy smokers underwent baseline screening with LDCT; 2553 participants were diagnosed with pulmonary nodules. Detailed questionnaire, physical assessment and follow-up were completed for all participants. Multivariable Cox proportional risk regression models were used to identify and integrate key prognostic factors for the development of a nomogram model. Data from the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) were utilized for external validation. Results A total of 111 lung cancer cases with a median follow-up duration of 3.7 years occurred in the Henan CanSPUC. Age, gender, physical activity, consumption of pickled food, history of silicosis or pneumoconiosis, nodule type, size, calcification, and pleural retraction sign were included into the model. The AUC was 0.855, 0.844, and 0.863 for the 1-, 3- and 5-year lung cancer risk in the training set, respectively. Compared with Mayo model, VA model, PKU model, and Brock model, the Henan CanSPUC model yield statistically better discriminatory performance (all P values < 0.05). The model calibrated well across the deciles of predicted risk in both the overall population and all subgroups. The model demonstrated good calibration and discrimination in the internal validation cohort, while the external validation cohort showed lower predictive performance, indicating that further external validation is needed. Conclusions The model developed and validated in this study may be used to estimate the probability of lung cancer in nodules detected at baseline LDCT, allowing more efficient risk-adapted follow-up in population-based LCS programs. However, further external validation in broader and more diverse populations is warranted.
